analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from using AI and personal surveillance data to set individualized prices and wages.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 23, 2025 with 41 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to three House committees and has seen no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for companies to use automated systems fed by surveillance data — things like a person's location history, health signals, or browsing behavior — to set a custom price for one shopper or a custom wage for one worker. It carves out legitimate practices like cost-based differences and disclosed discounts for groups such as seniors or students, and allows wage tools that consider only local cost of living. It gives the Federal Trade Commission and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission power to enforce the ban, lets state attorneys general and individuals sue violators for at least $3,000 per violation, and invalidates pre-dispute arbitration clauses for these claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who would otherwise be quoted higher prices because of what data brokers know about them, and workers whose pay, hours, or task assignments are set by algorithms crunching personal information. Privacy-protective businesses that do not engage in surveillance pricing would also face less undercutting from competitors that do.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers and workers priced by their data

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits using automated decision systems and surveillance data to set customized prices or wages for specific people, with exceptions only for cost-based differences, publicly disclosed group discounts, and affirmatively enrolled loyalty programs [S2].
Allows automated wage tools only if they rely solely on the worker's city or state and its cost of living, blocking pay-setting based on personal data like health, location, or behavior [S2].

Gives the FTC enforcement power over price-setting violations (including over common carriers and nonprofits normally outside its reach) and gives the EEOC enforcement power over wage-setting violations, on top of state attorney general suits and private lawsuits with at least $3,000 per violation [S2].

Invalidates pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers between companies and consumers or workers for claims under the bill, so victims can go to court instead of being forced into private arbitration [S2].

Preserves collective bargaining rights, requires employers to bargain over any use of automated systems to set compensation under an existing union contract, and lets state laws that are stronger survive [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that use AI-driven personalized pricing or algorithmic wage-setting, the data brokers selling the underlying personal information, and the arbitration industry, which loses forced-arbitration claims under this law. Some compliance costs could be passed to consumers in the form of uniform (non-personalized) pricing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and AI pricing firms

drawbacks.text: The definitions are broad: 'surveillance data' covers nearly any information linked to a person, so the ban could sweep in pricing practices that many businesses consider ordinary data use, requiring significant compliance changes [S2].
The private right of action offers a minimum $3,000 recovery per violation, and critics of such statutory damages argue they can drive litigation costs that ultimately show up in prices [S2].

Banning individualized pricing also bans individualized discounts that could benefit some consumers: only publicly disclosed group discounts and affirmatively enrolled loyalty programs are preserved, so other data-driven deals would end [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection — no quoting you a higher price or a lower wage because an algorithm profiled you — addresses a real and growing practice, and the bill is drafted to spare cost-based pricing, disclosed discounts, and cost-of-living pay tools. The honest tradeoffs are compliance cost and litigation risk from broad definitions and statutory damages. On balance the benefit to consumers and workers outweighs those costs, though the enforcement value depends heavily on regulators actually using the new powers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sits with three House committees, which have taken no action on it since it was referred on the day it was introduced.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Casar, joined by Rep. Rashida Tlaib, introduced the bill in the House on July 23, 2025 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, and Education and Workforce [S4].
41 House Democrats — all of the bill's cosponsors — signed on; no Republican cosponsors appear [S3].
The action history shows no hearings, markups, or votes since the referral, while Congress remains in session [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened, the status quo holds: companies using AI-driven personalized pricing and algorithmic wage-setting, and the data brokers supplying them, keep operating unchanged. Consumers and workers have gained nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: AI pricing firms and data brokers, so far

sides.party_line_note: All 41 cosponsors are Democrats, with no Republican support on record, in a House where Republicans hold 223 of 440 seats [S3].

industries.note: These firms sell the personal, behavioral, and location data that surveillance pricing runs on; the ban cuts off that use and lets people sue for at least $3,000 per violation. Their business model profits from exactly the profiling the bill prohibits.

industries.industry: Retailers, travel, and e-commerce platforms using personalized pricing
industries.note: The bill bars quoting a custom price based on what the company knows about a shopper — a practice that lets firms capture the maximum each customer will pay. Uniform pricing rules mean some consumers pay less, while the company loses that price discrimination.

industries.industry: Algorithmic wage-setting and gig-platform software providers
industries.note: Pay tools that set wages, schedules, and task assignments using personal data would be barred, allowed only to use local cost of living. Workers whose pay is algorithmically driven gain the protection.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and employers relying on arbitration clauses
industries.note: The bill voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for claims under it, so disputes must go to court. This shrinks the market for forced arbitration in pricing and wage cases.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action since July 2025 and no Republican cosponsors in a Republican-controlled House, the bill's likely path is to remain stalled in committee for the rest of the Congress, as most single-sponsor bills do. It could advance only if it attracts bipartisan support or leadership decides to prioritize it, neither of which appears likely.
